I'm not using concentrated extracts or chemically modified products sold in gas stations. Yet the article barely distinguishes those products from the natural plant, despite potentially enormous differences in potency and risk.

Of course kratom carries risks. So do alcohol and tobacco, which cause enormous numbers of deaths annually. Yet we regulate those products rather than prohibit them, even though they arguably lack the therapeutic benefits of kratom.

There is a legitimate debate to be had about regulating concentrated extracts, synthetic derivatives, adulterated products, and sales to minors. But the dangers of those products shouldn't be conflated with those of ordinary ground leaves.

Articles like these invariably focus on the plight of renters and frequently portray all landlords as predatory. Perhaps some are, but that characterization ignores the reality facing many small landlords.

I inherited a small rental condo in the Brighton neighborhood of Boston. Since 2021, property taxes have increased by 29%, condo fees by 73%, and insurance premiums by a whopping 166%, not including a couple of special assessments that ran into thousands of dollars. Meanwhile, rent, which wasn’t particularly high to begin with, has increased by only 18% over the past five years.

According to a national Zillow survey, 84% of American landlords own fewer than five rental properties. Most landlords are not large corporations or institutional investors, yet discussions of housing affordability routinely overlook the escalating costs borne by small property owners. Landlords are expected to absorb ever-rising expenses while being portrayed as the villains whenever rents increase. From my experience with technology, including earlier versions of AI, inventors and promoters often hype it far beyond what’s reasonable or achievable in the short and medium term, and even knowable in the long term. This is compounded by their strange warnings about end-of-the-world scenarios, which seem tied to both the hype and the desire to avoid liability from negligent behavior, as well as competition from newcomers, while placing themselves at the mercy of governments.

Given this, the addressable market will likely be much smaller than claimed, divided and segmented among many competitors and applications. The most expensive cutting-edge models, such as those from Anthropic, could face severe limitations in commercial use due to government restrictions on national security grounds.

That said, AI is genuinely revolutionary, promising a welcome boost in productivity and enabling countless new discoveries in science and technology. However, it will take time, and the rewards will be shared among many stakeholders, with pioneers not necessarily reaping the majority of benefits.

"Humans can think in only three dimensions — height, width and depth. "  I strongly disagree and it conflates the very basis ( pardon the pun) upon which AI is founded.  Simply learning to walk demands mastery of where(x,y,z) ,when(time), and orientation(3 angles). Orientation is an important  degree of freedom, assuming you intend to walk upright.   7 dimensions and that's just getting started and it's not at all hard to interprete.

From a LLM perspective, this comment can be 1500 words long (a vector). Each word an independent dimension (location within comment) with an entire dictionary of possible values. The words must be very carefully coupled over multiple lines or paragraphs or pages if they are to tell a compelling story.  
Gibberish is the result of ignoring these couplings.

From this perspective authors, story tellers, artists and humans in general are very highly dimensional thinkers that maintain engaging "statistical relations" across volumes while AI can easily drift in a paragraph of two.  Is AI  super human or just getting started?

Don't sell us short.

So, why would we know how these artificial intelligence systems work, let alone how they will behave? Much of the language we use to talk about these systems is nonsense. There is no such thing as alignment (we can’t get two humans to agree) let alone the interest of humanity. Anything that’s based on human knowledge will bake in all the contradictions and failings of humanity that are an essential part of humanity itself.

As a practical matter, LLMs are most useful as a human-language interface. LLMs should—at best—delegate real and meaningful work to other AI systems that are more domain-specific, deterministic, and transparent and keep humans in the loop.

Enjoyed the humor as I started my day but the message is important. For anyone involved in activities like dance, singing and sports, understanding how to use one's breath is paramount to performing well.

A relative of mine was asked after surviving a widowmaker cardiac arrest whether they had had a sleep study (they had not). Sleep deprivation can also cause serious changes in cognitive performance that are confused with dementia but clear up with treatment. A feature of natural nose breathing is that your body switches the flow from one side to the other within the nasal cavity roughly every 20 minutes. This gives the other side a rest.
There's more good science out there on nose breathing,

Belly breathe WHILE expanding your lower ribcage, lower back and mid back. I had long wondered why belly breathing didn’t help me. A physical therapist noticed my lower ribcage wasn’t expanding when I breathed even though my belly was expanding.

It could be when belly breathing most people expand their ribcage naturally which is why it’s never mentioned. But for those of us who don’t, belly breathing just reinforces bad breathing habits. It takes concentration to break that tension habit and expand the ribcage side to side, across the back and expand the back muscles.

Then when breathing out, don’t just pull your belly button in, tighten the lower back muscles. It should also naturally pull your posture straighter.

I watch the rising highest highs in Del Mar’s lagoons and along the Potomac River on the Virginia side. 

Del Mar: On Monday, there were waves in the Penasquitos Lagoon. The lagoon was as full as I have ever seen it — pure water, no sand or grass showing through all along Carmel Valley Road to the highway. The water lapped at the road Right Of Way. 

Westmoreland: Where the Potomac meets the Bay, the highest highs can be monitored with the private piers along the shoreline in places like Colonial Beach. Rarely have the piers been under the water in the past. Going forward, we shall see. 

As others have commented, it is the variability, not the mean, that we must plan for.

comments.body: Crystal Bridges is one of the least user-friendly museums I've ever visited.  A single narrow entrance leading to an elevator without adequate signage.  Most of the parking is a shuttle-bus journey away.  There is little covered parking close by (excruciating in the middle of summer).   If you get there early, before the museum opens there is no shade to stand in, so one literally broils in the hot sun. Doesn't WalMart sell shade-sails?  Confusing layout and inadequate signage throughout, which is very hard on those with limited mobility since you waste energy when finding the areas you want to be.  Virtually no seating for tired patrons and the few comfy chairs have wheels, which makes them hard to rise from without the chair careening across the polished floors.   Exhibits are clustered in absurd groups, making it difficult to figure out which label (sometimes yards away) applies to which painting.  The exhibits at the top of those clusters is hard to look at, and makes appreciation impossible for children, those in wheelchairs or the vertically-challenged.  Expensive cafes that add considerably to the cost of a visit.   It's lovely to look at, but too clever by half.  One gets the impression of a museum run by rich amateurs . . . funny, that.

This news is deeply moving...
Decades ago, when I was teaching middle school,  I attended a statewide, social studies conference. Dolores Huerta was a keynote speaker. I'll never forget one of her pieces of advice to us, along the lines of "Be sure to always wash the produce you buy." In addition to the hard work in the fields, many migrant laborers didn't always have access to toilets or handwashing facilities. 
She ended her by getting an enormous crowd of teachers, cheering and chanting, "Viva la Causa!" 
All these years since, maybe conditions have improved. Yet always on a long drive in rural California, I notice workers in the fields. I'm reminded of Dolores Huerta and waving my arms and chanting with others. Even today I pause when tempted to buy grapes, due to the endless years of boycotts.

A public vigil in her honor is probably not too hard in the Bay Area. I'll be there with a candle in her honor.

I first became a fan of Jimmy while living in the Tahoe area in the early 1970’s. He was playing at a small venue in Squaw Valley, the Hofbrau, but I got there late and it was sold out. A bunch of us gathered on the deck outside and partied with the muffled sound of his tunes. 
A few years later, at my wedding, some friends and I sang “Why don’t we get drunk…” and dedicated it to my new wife. She is truly amazing as we are still married 46 years later! We’ve been to his shows many times, taking our kids, who also became parrot heads. What 10 year old wouldn’t love a giant inflatable shark flying overhead as the crowd does fins to the left, fins to the right?
Fast forward to Sept. 1, 2023. I’m at Burning Man and a nearby camp is having a Cheesburger in Paridise party. My wife, daughter and I cruise in to join the Buffett sing along. Most of the crowd was Gen Z and oblivious to his songs, just coming for the free burgers. The 3 of us had a good time, as we knew all the lyrics to all the songs, as most  parrot heads do. It wasn’t until we got home that we heard that’s the day he passed away. 
RIP Jimmy, you will live on in the hearts of many.

The problem is not so much that a crooked president can abuse the powers of the DOJ, but that the DOJ allowed a crooked conman to attain the presidency.  The DOJ's traditional 90% conviction rate indicates that they have been prosecuting the easy cases not the important ones.  Trump's idea of what is important is all wrong, but the principle is not. It takes political will to hold the rich and powerful to account to prevent the corrupt from ascending in our society.

Indictments should be sought whenever there is plausible evidence of wrongdoing. If the perpetrator is seeking political office, that is all the more reason to heighten scrutiny, not treat them with kid gloves as has been precedent. Given all of the protections our courts provide to the accused, not bringing charges unless conviction is likely amounts to immunity for the rich and powerful. 

Our legal system is designed to let 10 guilty men go free before 1 innocent is convicted.  That doesn't mean that 10 guilty men should be president before one innocent is denied the position. Voters must ultimately decide who is qualified to be president, but our law enforcement system can use their powers of investigation and truth finding to better insure that they are well informed.

comments.name: Daniel De Simone
comments.body:
"The subject and the director are trying to manipulate each other, outdo each other. It feels less organic as a result.."

This is the case in every documentary. Subjects, particularly controversial ones, are trying to control how they are perceived through the director, and directors query their subjects in such a way to create a compelling story.

You Can See Everything just takes that unacknowledged subtext of the form and makes it text.

comments.name: Edgar Sanchez
comments.body:
When this movie came out, I vowed not to see it due to my fears that it would glamorize E. Holmes, a first-class criminal.
Then, something unusual happened:  A friend who had seen "You Can See Everything," raved about it, with words that included, "It does not glamorize Elizabeth Holmes."
He urged me to view the film.
And so, I broke my vow.  Earlier today, I watched "You Can See Everything."  I went from hating a film to thoroughly enjoying it.  And no, it does not glorify Holmes, who unfortunately will soon be transferred from prison to a halfway house.  She should remain in prison for many more years.

comments.name: David Robinson
comments.body: Serious question: What is a documentary, then, if "You Can See Everything" isn't one?

comments.name: Tj
comments.body: I've seen it twice--cant stop thinking about it, talking about it, reading about it and writing about it. Whatever this film is, I don't think there's a word for it. articles.title: Could ‘You Can See Everything’ Be Up for Best Picture but Not Documentary?

comments.name: Ruthie Sarnoski
comments.body: Although technology can be distracting, it’s important to have it during our education. In my opinion the good outweighs the harm of having computers or tablets in classrooms. Eliminating technology from classrooms can have a series of negative impacts on students. As technology advances it’s important for current students and future adults to have digital literacy. Not having digital literacy can prevent and get in the way of jobs and life. Another reason to keep technology in schools is the access to technology. For many students school-issued devices are the only technology they have access to at home. The more we embrace technology the more students will grow into the world of technology.

comments.name: Cecily Miller
comments.body: I hate to say it, I think having no technology or at least a limit on screen time in class would benefit students. Technology is very helpful and convenient for things as a student, like typing online and the ease of turning assignments in. Also access to technology can help learning in general with the amount of resources you have. While technology is great for those things, students abuse that privledge on the computer by doing stuff off task like playing games. I don’t use technology in every class at school, which I’m happy about because I think I’d hate having it all digital, but a good amount of my classes do use it. I don’t think we should completely take away digital learning because we live in a day and age where technology and knowing how to use it is important. While some schools do have a computer class where they can learn how to use them, I feel like the use of technology implemented in your everyday life (or at least at school), can help you learn how to navigate and use technology. Especially for the use of productivity like typing docs or writing emails. I do think it is important for there to be a limit, maybe 2 hours, because every student can have a different amount of time spent on a screen outside of school. Technology can be very helpful in education and we’ve seen proof of that whether it’s turning in assignments, checking grades easily, or during Covid, but I do think there should be limits for the well-being of students education and mental health.

comments.name: Avi George
comments.body: My opinion is that technology is more helpful than harmful. Technology can help us get work done faster, deliver emails to teachers, and can even help us become more productive. Technology can help our skills improve in our everyday academic lives and even our lives later on. The students' desire is to not do work. Thus leading them to defy teacher restrictions. I do agree that screen time can be bad but it can be just as beneficial.

comments.name: Corinne Gazda
comments.body:
I think technology in classrooms does more good than harm. There are many reasons, including that we can do work at home, learn more, and easily organize our assignments. I have no homework on paper, and almost all school work online. This is helpful because I can take it home and check if I have assignments. Having everything in one place is very helpful to me. I don’t have to carry many different papers and risk them getting lost or damaged. No one can say, “The dog ate my homework.” 
Computers are very helpful when doing research or trying to learn more. We can look up facts without having to wait for a very specific book in the library, watch a video on a topic instead of working extra during lunch, or make a presentation without needing huge signs. My school uses a program that blocks us from certain websites or games. While students can still find ways around it, I find the extra precaution somewhat stops it and finalizes the fact that the benefits of technology outweigh the harms.

comments.name: Vihaan Modi
comments.body: I think that the benefits of technology are that everything is digital so you can easily access sources of information so if you forget a textbook you can always access it digitally. Another benefit of technology is that you can type everything and do not have to worry about writing by hand. I think that the drawbacks of technology are that in class students can access YouTube videos and video games and easily get distracted in class and go off-task. I think that technology in class does make it harder for students to stay on-task because it distracts them from the focus of the class, separating them from the learning process and the education that they receive. It does affect how much my classmates and I engage with each other because this is another form of distraction from the focus of the class.

comments.name: Jonah S.
comments.body: I think some of the drawbacks of less technology is the fact that it’s hard to manage students. In my school, lots of students will play video games when they aren’t supposed to. There are resources like GoGuardion, but it never fully stops the problem. Every time there are workarounds that you can never fully get rid of. However, one of the benefits of having technology is that it is easier to assign work, and it’s much easier for teachers to receive work. For example, with online work, there is never a problem of forgetting a paper at home, or not having a sheet of paper. With technology, in just the click of a button you can turn in the work digitally. Another very important benefit for students is that you don’t have to carry around a ton of papers, and search through photos for that one assignment that's due. It makes it easier for me personally because I can type extremely quickly, and I’ve been taught how to type by my teachers. Not only that, typing is always going to be easier and faster than writing. For me it doesn’t really make it harder to stay on task, however for some students I know it is challenging for them. It never affects how I communicate with other students, and I can do the work at my own pace easily. One thing I don’t like about computers is the due dates on assignments get shortened to late at night instead of when school starts. It makes it so I can’t do assignments in the morning if I can't finish them at night. Overall, technology is good and bad.

comments.name: Foster Garonzik
comments.body: According to the FCC, over 50% of all school students past 8th grade use devices in class frequently. And is this a problem? It really depends. For example, if you use a lot of device time in class but for good use, then it's not so bad but it still is.  On the other hand, we have people who constantly go off task and the whole device thing just creates very big temptations to do other things which isn’t helpful for your education. If you use your phone or school-issued computer, it creates the temptation to play games or go on social media. Although, I do think a majority of this is because of Covid-19. Staying inside for months with nothing but electronics and pencils we didn’t see a use in. And I believe that because of this, started the uprising of the addiction to social media. But, if I was a teacher, and I saw this occurring problem, I would do something about it. But my limit wouldn’t be a set time, it would just be to close the computer or phone when you are done your work.

comments.name: Darren
comments.body: If I was a teacher I would make sure my students would be able to go on their computers but I want them to use it only when needed unless it's like a free period to chill and talk. I wouldn't let them use it in the beginning of class unless they are doing the world or a game on the New York Times but I know people are gonna sneak on other games so it's questionable. I've seen and sometimes but not usually go on my chromebook when I get to class but there's usually instructions as we walk in. So I would have rules just not super strict rules and I would try to be prepared myself.

There is nothing saying that just because they have money today that they will have it tomorrow and be expecting  hand out because they are entitled.

Maybe if we stopped deficit spending our way into bankruptcy with our attempt at maintaining EMPIRE, and actually had a tax system that favors fairness rather than the ultra-rich, things would be different. We have a socialist government, it's just socialism for the ultra wealthy and debt slavery for the poor. Pitchforks and torches anybody?

comments.name: Mark
comments.body:
The article points out that Social Security contributions have two components, one from the employer and one from the employee. In my view the cap should be eliminated for the employer’s contribution, since it should be seen as a business expense associated with hiring employees.  As it stands, a company that hires a ceo for 100,000,000 dollars a year only pays taxes on the first 185,000, or 12,500 dollars.  If the same company hires 1000 employees at 100,000 a piece, the company will pay payroll taxes on all of their earnings, or 6.2 million.  This seems unfair to me, since it would make it cheaper to hire one fat cat, rather than offer employment to many.

I’d be more hesitate to raise the cap on the employee. Unless you are willing to raise the payout that the employee receives for additional contributions, payroll taxes will be seen as purely a tax by high earners, and this will erode the almost universal support program has when it is viewed as an earned benefit.  In effect, Social Security would become another welfare program.

I was fortunate enough to play Kaffee last year in a community theatre production of A Few Good Men. It was a fun and difficult play to do, and Kaffee is a great role for an actor to seek his teeth into. (I had quite a few people tell me I was better than Tom Cruise in the role. Italy’s problems with corruption have long been among the most serious in Europe. Its economy has stagnated, and real wages have barely increased over the past three decades.

Other countries, such as Spain, have been more effective and innovative in addressing their challenges. For example, Spain has diversified its energy mix by investing heavily in solar and wind power.

Italy, by contrast, seems more inclined to complain to the EU about no longer being able to rely on Russian gas than to pursue a more ambitious strategy for energy independence.

Ultimately, many of the root causes of Italy’s problems lie within the country itself, and addressing them requires domestic reforms rather than blaming external factors.

This also reminds me of a large portion of the protests of the 1960s here in the US - it felt good to be part of the cause, but few people put anything serious on the line to make real change - instead, they retreated to their comfortable middle-class lives - the result being that we still have the same destructive capitalism and elitism that have brought us to this point.

"How Israel’s Election Looks to Its Neighbours?"

I don't think it looks very democratic to Israel’s neighbours or even many Israelis themselves.  The main reason for that is, in order to become part of the government and have any power, the parties need to align themselves with the party that is trying to form the government. It is worth noting that policies of these parties are sufficiently different from each other, to the point that justify forming a separate party.

In practice that means, to join the top party, other parties are forced to make compromises on their own key policies.  The abandoned policies are often the same policies that were attractive to voters who voted for these parties.   So, in many cases, the machinations that goes on after the election leads to betrayal of Israeli voters.

In San Francisco (and I’m guessing probably NY, too), Air BnB continues to crowd out the older, smaller units that used to be housing for the city’s service industry workers. Meanwhile luxury condominiums sell every unit, but sit half vacant since they only function as pied-a-tiers and investment properties for wealthy foreign investors. If I thought that luxury housing units were going to bring down costs for waiters, baristas, teachers, social workers, and that poor family living in a tent under the highway, I’d support the building of luxury units in a heartbeat. Maybe then you wouldn’t have to fight the NIMBY neighbors. Instead, these units are often transparently built—like every other aspect of our economy—to benefit the wealthiest people on earth and the slightly less wealthy people who are trying to join the ranks of the ultra-rich. NIMBYism is sometimes just another word for a functioning representative democracy that frustrates developers who are trying to get richer. There are genuine affordable housing projects built by private companies that actually house working people and people who are unable to work—those are great. But "housing of any kind" does not lower rents at present. There must be regulatory control to evict AirBnb and investors who are misusing the housing stock.

If Vučić genuinely wanted an ironclad grip on power, he should have taken a masterclass from India in how to systematically hollow out an election before polling day even begins. Rather than scramble against high turnout, Indian authorities have mastered bureaucratic disenfranchisement—exemplified by the recent Special Intensive Revision (SIR) controversy, where over a hundred million names were purged from draft rolls under the guise of automated “revisions,” alongside steep procedural hurdles designed to suppress new and minority voters. Had Belgrade studied this playbook, Serbia’s youth wouldn't have been celebrating at the ballot box; they would have spent election day standing outside locked polling booths, finding their registrations conveniently erased by clerical decree.

I had a side hustle as a reviewer of horror fiction back in the 1990s & 2000s. It was a source of irritation back then that chains like Barnes & Noble and Borders had dedicated science fiction sections, but horror books were scattered through General Fiction and Literary. 

I used to recommend drugstores as the places to buy horror, since they had ample racks of mass market horror. Easy to find because they were all shiny black with touches of red, with gaudy embossed silver lettering.

The quoted 39% increase in sales from one year to the next doesn't sound right. I think it's more likely that they changed the classification of books that are borderline horror—like dark fantasy. Another possible reason is that they included more horror marketed to kids and young adults.

comments.body: MANY a summer, often at night, I and my marine invertebrate students would gather on floating docks throughout WA State, especially on Whidbey Island, spending hours discovering all the many invertebrates living on and under those docks.  The presence of so many organisms on those docks, along with species we were seeing in various tide pools, added greatly to our "list of species seen" for that summer field course.  It was so much fun, and allowed for close connections to develop between me and my students.  Some of the most fun, memorable and interesting field excursions we had during those summers happened at the floating docks, both day and night.  With wet, cold, stiff hands and fingers, runny noses, and lots of "OH, look at this!" events that always got us heading to our home base late, we enjoyed every minute of our explorations.  This article brought back lots of fond memories.  Nice to read of others also enjoying this way of exploring an amazing marine habitat, where many might not think to look.

I've assumed that she was on the spectrum since she was a preteen, but she only just discovered it for herself and announced it to her family.  As far as I can tell, it was a relief for her to discover that she's not a "retard" and a failure, but rather suffers a common medical condition along with so many others.  I hope that she finds the support and community that she didn't get from her parents.

comments.name: VPM
comments.body:
I could not disagree more with your advice against telling this man that his dysfunction in life is almost certainly due to his mother's contracting rubella while she was pregnant with him.

First, given the description of his problems, it seems extremely likely - almost certain - that his many failures are due to the consequences of an infection. Second, his relatively high level of development clearly does not preclude his feelings of inadequacy and guilt about those failures. 

Perhaps the most common question that people in his situation ask themselves is Why am I such a failure? Why on earth would you NOT give him some relief from those feelings?

I am extremely disappointed with your lack of empathy for the very difficult life that this man has led. If this is where ethics leads us, I'll do without.

comments.name: Andante
comments.body:
When I went to do pre-pregnancy counseling, the doctor recommended I get a measles vaccine, even though I’d had it as a child. He said that the consequences of an infection could be so severe that I shouldn’t rely on my memory of my childhood illnesses. Unfortunately we’re now seeing how smart he was.

I feel so bad for the sister. She’s likely my age and didn’t get such good advice. Of course she feels guilty, even if it had nothing to do with measles. The OP needs to talk to HER about it—it should be her decision. She may not have thought about how this knowledge could potentially benefit her son. 

And it could. People often see such disabilities as more of a moral failing than anything physical.

"As far as you know", he hasn't been told? So his mother may have already told him, and you're unaware because none of this is your business?

Better to stay in your lane and stay out of this family's business.

comments.name: Huh?
comments.body:
“I suppose there’s a scenario in which your theory might come as a relief to him; l…
…
I’m not persuaded that your speculative explanation counts as an important fact.”

Mr. Appia, please imagine this:

*I am not able to do what most other people do. I am not able to do  most other people expect me to do. I have lost my spouse, alienated my kids, been fired again and again, and lived in the streets.*

*Am I defective?*

*Am I cursed?*

*Am I out of favor with my God?*

*Am I, like Job, being made to suffer for some unknown purpose?* 

*Should I keep striving?*

*Should I keep trying?*

*Should I admit defeat?*

*Should I end it now?*

Many people with ADHD, ASD, anxiety, depression, low IQ, and dozens of other disorders have had conversations like  with themselves again and again as again. If you never have, count yourself among the  ery fortunate. 

The possibility of C.R.S. is “an important fact” for this man. Any information which may help explain his lot in life is important. Countless people have been relieved by information or a diagnosis that helped them see themselves in a new light. Don’t withhold this information. He deserves to know the truth about his own life.

comments.name: BeenThere

One good guiding principle for a happy & ethical life: never discuss someone else’s diagnosis, particularly from 30 years ago. 
It’s not your business. 
It is not your job to tell him. 
Your sister already feels guilty. 

Everyone who gossips feels justified and they defend their impulse with some imagined “right to know.”  No such right exists. We’re each entitled to privacy with regard to medical information and those things we discuss with our therapists, pastors or attorneys. Respect your sister’s right.

I've traveled a few times for races and these are all great tips for anyone who wants to do so. However, I encourage any runner - new or seasoned - to include casual runs into their travel! My husband and I always plan to run when we travel - whether we're finding trails to explore or city streets, it's such a great way to see new places! When we're visiting a city, we wake up early and get out when the streets are still quiet. It's a great time of day and we often find interesting places we want to go back to and see more of later in the day. You can cover a lot of ground on the run and get to places you might not otherwise! The gear does require space in the luggage, but in my opinion, it's worth it!

As an alternative to large races, check out ParkRun.com! They're fun, free, volunteer-led 5ks in cities around the world. You get to run in local parks with local runners and make new acquaintances!

comments.name: Paul Sheldon
comments.body: Thanks for this book review. Socialism requires broad support which is challenged in this country by a small minority of extremely wealthy individuals who exert much control of what we see and hear and thus think. I have voted for Eugene Debs for President and Norman Thomas as Vice President, via write in vote, at those times when the proffered candidates (controlled by agreement between two parties in power) are hopeless.  The oldest socialist party in this country, the Socialist Labor Party, has an interesting plan that is clear and able to be updated to current times. Like Debs, they combine one big transparent democratic union with political candidates. A peaceful group of working-class men and women, such organizations have been squashed by those in power. It is good that we are starting to hear about peaceful socialism again.

comments.name: Chevy
comments.body:
Ranked-choice voting and its several variants would go a long way toward establishing multiple political parties of many different stripes.

It is hard to see how we could achieve a parliamentary system under our present Constitution, however.  We have a system of government that did not anticipate political parties and yet they formed immediately and have shifted over the course of American history - both in number and in ideology - ending up with two which have locked in their dominance.

This has resulted in an "either-or " choice between Democrats and Republicans, a choice which has become a chasm in the national political dialogue, a choice which has resulted in either blind obedience to a demagogue like Trump or an abhorrence to that for which he stands and our automatic support to whomever will stand up to oppose him.

comments.name: PWR
comments.body:
I would be interested in reading the Debs biography but the idea that there still is an industiral working class in this country that might "seize the means of production" is a romantic anachronism left over from the 19th century.  We have a service economy and we import hard goods. We don't have that many "workers" anymore; we have employees.  The manufacturing sector in the U.S. accounts for 9.7% of the economy and in New York State, it's only 3'5%.  Much of the "working class", like mechanics, electricians, plumbers, etc. run their own businesses.  They are capitalists. 

The socialist model no longer fits. It's no wonder that the Democratic Socialist party members are largely young, college educated, idealist and often underemployed with little practical life experience.  Their idea of socialism, it seems to me anyway, is one of financial redistribution that benefits them. dressed up as economic justice.

As an interesting point, failed European democratic revolts in Europe, Germany in particular, spurred immigration to the US midwest. These new immigrants were sympathetic to socialism and workers’ rights.

comments.name: Michael McBrearty
comments.body: One response to the interesting question as to why there is no socialism in America is that, under the Smith Act, from 1948 until 1957, teaching Marxism in America was as illegal as robbing a bank (and over 120 Communist Party leaders were sent to Federal prison for violating it). Even today,  Anti-communism is America's religion.  Fascism and Communism are depicted as extremist in comparison with the two party political consensus "centrism," i.e., neo liberal austerity and cutbacks combined with a crash program for preparation for war. Youth around the globe are employing social media to challenge this dismal future. In the long run, Social Media  = Socialism.

As far as the question of  “Why is there no socialism in America?”, I think the hijacking and distortion of socialism by the Russian Bolsheviks and the disaster that was Russia and it’s antipathy towards the U.S. must be a huge part of the answer.

comments.name: Paul Zarembka
comments.body:
Neither the article nor comments have referred to Debs’ strong opposition to U.S. participation in imperialist wars like WWI. That was the reason he was in jail in 1920 during the Presidential election. 

Lincoln as a young Whip member of the House opposed what we call the Mexican-American war of 1846-1848.  He asked whether, under President Polk, we had provoked the war in order to gain territory.  Yet, even with that conspiracy consideration, a quarter century later and much else to consider, Lincoln became President.  Debs, on the other hand, was already 61 when the U.S. entered WWI (he died in 1926) and the U.S. was now a different country than Lincoln’s.

History is complicated and knowing it accurately it is very important.

comments.name: Tom
comments.body: A fine review of the biography of a genuine American hero.  One of my closest friends is named after him.  The government used every means at its disposal to shut Debs down, including incarceration, but his spirit lives and continues to inspire.

comments.name: OneView
comments.body:
100 years ago, all pricing was by negotiation based on the individual and market conditions.  Shoppers (women and servants mostly) haggled and negotiated.  You can still find markets in Europe where the price is arrived at by agreement. We act like "dynamic pricing" is something "new" when it's as old as the first barter exchange between humans.

Of course, if you post a price, you need to sell at that price.  So that's a separate question.

comments.name: MG
comments.body: Not only are there "errors" at check out, but frequently products in food markets are not even marked. It's hard enough to suss out a product re ingredients, size of package/packaging, "best by" dates...but to additionally try and find a price is asking a lot of a shopper. And what about non-food retail? I sweater is "$159 but on sale for $89" (for example) - we know those numbers have nothing to do with cost of production + shipping + displaying + other costs + profit /%. They are engineered to the umpteenth degree to get us to think we're getting a bargain. It all sucks.

Everything about it was glorious: the photography, the writing, the breadth of topics from the Mets in the World Series to a platoon on patrol in Vietnam - even the full-color ads for gas-guzzling cars and cigarette brands we're well crafted. comments.body: In June,1970, I had just graduated college, and got a job with a Big 8 accounting firm in Manhattan. Alas, I also had a low draft lottery number, and was scheduled to report for boot camp in mid-August. Several of my friends were in exactly the same situation, and we needed some affordable, temporary housing. We came across a suite of rooms in an elegant but dilapidated old hotel near Montague Street (Hotel St. George?) that was mostly unoccupied, except for a few really old and creepy long term tenants. Our neighborhood bar was a place called Capulets on Montague, a very "Cheers" type of place. Mugs of cold beer, good chili, and pretty waitresses. Ah, those were the days, my friends!

comments.body:
As a Mac user, thoroughly entrenched in their echo system, including iPads, the lack of a touch screen option on their laptops often seemed odd. I know other Mac users who have long wanted the option. Still, I consider it a nice to have, not a must have, feature. 

For those touting that touch screens have long been available on PC laptops, I would note that they are still available on them but they are not as readily available at a good price as they used to be for high end models. I have to use a powerful PC laptop for chess programs (otherwise I would not deal with Windows) and when it came time to replace a model with the feature, I had to settle for a PC without it to get a more robust model at a relatively reasonable price. So they may not be as ubiquitous as they used to be in the PC world.

So, I'm content to wait until the v1 Duos are discounted, though with their hinge issues, I may waiting even longer than I think.

Anyway, still a fan, but not exactly racing to the website or online to order...

comments.body: For a school record to show only 30 students and a teacher recalling more like 45 makes more sense than not, said every public teacher everywhere.

comments.name: common sense advocate ⚖️
comments.body:
'There were kids that really didn’t want to be in the class, but he made sure to make it good for them and to have them be inspired and to want better,” she said. “For sixth grade, that was a lot. He didn’t have to do all of that'

And that's what Talarico is doing with politics too. He's committed to making the system work for the people of Texas who have been left behind - people who are hurting financially from the current administration, scared of disease spreading, and tired of hearing the hatred.

comments.name: Ellie
comments.body: As a 6th grade Teach For America teacher in a Dallas ISD school, I can absolutely relate to what James Talarico experienced in his classroom. Substitutes were rarely available at our Title 1 school, and classes were often split between other classrooms. This put a huge onus on teachers to try to accomplish their day's lesson plans while managing students who didn't have a place to sit and who may have been pretty thrown off by the change in their daily routine. Of course no official records would have documented these unofficial but absolutely real (and for too frequent) moments. For James to site one of these situations as informative to his career and his political values makes total sense to me.

comments.body: 45 looks a lot like two classrooms put together. Is it possible that this school was sometimes short on substitute teachers and classes were sometimes combined?

I suspect that the administrators at his school chose their class size data very carefully based on original enrollment rather than the number of kids who were dumped into the class. I see no reason not to believe Talarico’s account.

comments.name: CGR

comments.name: Guy Walker
comments.body: Are these bugs left by patent holders intentionally?  Like, do you think that all along software bugs are determined worth the time of rewriting if say there's a deadline for release to the consumer?  And that maybe they even vote whether these bugs are worth the time and effort or won't be noticed for a long time or that evil forces at work are planting bugs around like they drop cookies on Paul McCartney?

comments.name: William Wroblicka
comments.body: I wonder if the patched production-grade software is being properly tested before being re-released to its end users. In other words, what assurance is there that changes made to the code base to mitigate the vulnerability don't inadvertently introduce errors or cause the software to malfunction when put back in service? This happens all the time if/when testing is rushed or shortcuts are taken: You think you've fixed one problem in the software only to discover you've broken something somewhere else.

comments.name: MM
comments.body:
Mr. Prince said. “The next two years, it’s going to feel like the sky is falling, but I think we come out the other end of it with a much safer internet.”

This is the optimistic view.  

I suspect this will be an ongoing problem more like the security risk to personal online accounts (think passwords, 2-factor authentication, passkeys, etc).  Security is always a risk, always a hassle, an escalating war between hackers and users.  That's what we are facing, just with AI on both sides and us helpless in the middle.

comments.name: Peter Heimann
comments.body: Another example of how AI will create new jobs as well as destroying some existing ones.  Also another episode in the perennial story of "better lock-picker, better lock."

comments.name: Jack
comments.body: Remember "Life finds a way"? More and more powerful agents will find more flaws, which will be patched by even more and even more powerful agents that will then find additional flaws. This ratchet goes only one way. While the elephants enjoy their spy vs spy vs spy, games, the rest of us will lose all trust in truth, honesty and in systems that we've all grown to rely on.

comments.name: Steve
comments.body:
I'd like to know if the AI has created "exploits" to demonstrate that a bug can be used to significantly compromise a system or if most of these are fairly insignificant.  Maybe the bug can leak a user's geographic location or phone number, but not drain their bank account.

It's not unlike an AI company to put out a scary story like this to further convince us that AI is a super powerful tool that everyone needs to buy to keep themselves safe.

This is some good information, but I'm waiting for more before I start setting my hair on fire.

comments.name: Bow Farmer
comments.body:
The PHP2Shell vulnerability is difficult to exploit, but hackers are steadily making progress, with many sharing their efforts online. It is now a race against time for tens of millions of services running various versions of PHP, many so outdated that patching them is far from straightforward. These systems need to be secured before hackers develop reliable, widely usable exploits.

CISA, the Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency, has given federal agencies until October 29 to patch affected PHP systems or take other protective measures, including taking vulnerable systems offline or restricting external access.

comments.name: Kumar
comments.body:
Security vulnerabilities are  significant but are relatively easy to find. It is basically a global control flow and data flow analysis across the code base. Theoretically this is an undecidable problem. But advances in computing power and program analysis algorithms have vastly expanded the practical scope of discoveries. But there seem to be little relief for customers.  There is an explosion in customer experienced/found bugs. AI does not seem to help much (so far). Couple of days ago, NYT carried a review of  new Googlebook. https://www.nytimes.com/wirecutter/reviews/googlebooks-first-impressions/

This is a quote: "Though they’re nice laptops with bright displays, 
satisfying keyboards and trackpads, and solid build quality, don’t be fooled: The hardware is undermined by a buggy, unreliable operating system. In my weeks of testing, the Googlebooks proved to be littered with hints of good ideas that weren’t fully baked or were just poorly implemented."  Google is a major AI power.

comments.name: Publius
comments.body:
Having spent my career in what is now a smallish mid-size Los Angeles firm, I am not troubled by the comeuppances of the mega firms. Mine was the third oldest firm in LA when I joined it fifty years ago. It is a minnow now. But it has always stayed solid, despite some defections of a very few partners bought away by some of the mega firms. A big reason is that our firm recognized that we were professionals, not just entrepreneurs. We believed we were obliged to give back to our community in manifold ways. We paid our staff well, even as technology caused us to reduce their number. I was forced to retire for medical reasons many years ago, but the firm continues to thrive. 

The larger issue for me is whether law in this country is viable any longer. We have a POTUS who thinks he IS the law. We have a craven SCOTUS that has basically given him carte blanche. I would not be a lawyer today, despite the fact that I loved being one when I was. Because back then, the rule of law still worked. The social contract was still intact. All of that is gone. When everything becomes transactional and it's all about money, game over for me. Not a worthwhile way to live. Prove by the law firms who caved to the blackmail from the narcissist in chief. 

So forgive me if I do not mourn the demise of law firms that have sold their souls. They will not be missed.

The US companies then shrank dramatically or folded.

comments.name: Nogi Ichida
comments.body:
Chinese influence overseas is largely transactional, driven by economic interests. The hybrid system combining Communist Party rule with state capitalism still creates a lot of confusion for the outside world.

But the world has entered a new chapter. Many nations need to start thinking about how to deal with a country that soon becomes the world’s largest economy by nominal GDP.

If China were to buy a port in Japan or Canada, it probably wouldn’t be welcomed by the elephant in the room: the US. But in a country like Spain, which is not a geopolitical rival of China, such engagement could bring imminent benefits. China can offer manufacturing expertise, investment, and an influx of Chinese tourists.

Ultimately, it all comes down to how comfortable a country feels balancing its relationships, based on its geographic location, existing alliances, and cultural ties.

Spain, for its part, has plenty to offer China, from fruits and wine to foodand culture, industrial output as well. Nobody can say what the relationship will look like in 20 years, but over the next five to ten years, deeper economic engagement with China could be beneficial to Spain.

From the article: “With climate change helping to fuel a record expansion of the seaweed throughout the Caribbean and up the coast of the U.S. — reaching as far as North Carolina this summer — the Mexican efforts are being held up as a potential test case for a sustainable solution.”

As the surface of the ocean gets warmer, the water is lighter when it's warmer, it becomes harder and harder to turn the ocean over. We say it becomes more strongly stratified. 

The consequence of that is that all those nutrients from the deep ocean that fuel the great anchoveta fisheries, of the sardines of California or in Peru or whatever, those slow down their journey to the surface and those fisheries collapse. 

And, at the same time, water from the surface, which is rich in oxygen, doesn't make it down and the ocean turns into a desert.

This article makes the astonishing claim that ragtime marked the beginning of American popular music, particularly Black popular music. That overlooks more than a century of musical history.

Long before ragtime, African Americans had developed rich traditions of spirituals, work songs, field hollers, religious music, and dance. The Fisk Jubilee Singers brought spirituals to national and international audiences beginning in 1871. Blackface minstrelsy, drawing on and caricaturing Black musical traditions, became a major commercial entertainment industry in the 1840s.

Nor should we forget patriotic songs like “Yankee Doodle,” Stephen Foster's immensely popular minstrel and sentimental ballads, or the extraordinary outpouring of Civil War music, including “The Battle Hymn of the Republic” and “When Johnny Comes Marching Home.”

By the 1890s, America already possessed a flourishing popular music culture, supported by commercial publishers, touring performers, and a national market for sheet music.

Ragtime was a transformative achievement, particularly for Black composers and performers. But its importance needs no invented origin story. Ragtime revolutionized an existing musical culture, but it did not create American popular music—or Black popular music.

comments.name: Julia Angwin
comments.body: This summer, I started noticing that I felt hopeful and even a bit joyful after a bout of scrolling on my TikTok and Instagram feeds, compared to the depression and anger I often felt scrolling on X and Bluesky. I wondered if my experience was unique — and I stumbled onto this research showing that the video feed algorithms are optimized differently. This led me to wonder how it was affecting political discourse now that so much of our politics happens online. I’m curious if you all have noticed the same thing on your social video feeds?

articles.title: TikTok Is Changing Politics (Perhaps for the Better)
articles.summary: Algorithms are making politicians focus more on positive messaging in short video.
